1.s: On the plains of Moab Moses begins his farewell speeches, recalling how Israel refused to enter the land forty years before.
1.d: The whole book is set east of the Jordan, in Moab, on the eve of the crossing [[nabre:deuteronomy/1]]. It follows the pattern of an ancient covenant treaty, but it is mainly a series of speeches by Moses [[tosn:Deuteronomy 1:1]]. Chapters 1–3 retell events found, with some differences, in Numbers [[nabre:deuteronomy/1]].

2.s: The journey past Edom, Moab and Ammon, Israel’s relatives, and the defeat of Sihon.
2.d: God gave lands to Edom, Moab and Ammon too, not only to Israel [[tosn:Deuteronomy 2:5]]. Moab and Ammon were Israel’s relatives, so Israel was not to fight them; Ruth, David’s great-grandmother, came from Moab [[tosn:Deuteronomy 2:9]].

3.s: The defeat of Og and the settlement east of the Jordan. Moses pleads to enter the land, but God says no.
3.d: Pisgah is part of the Abarim range, and its highest peak is Mount Nebo, where Moses later views the land and dies [[tosn:Deuteronomy 3:17]] [[bible:Deuteronomy 34:1]]. Scripture gives different reasons why Moses could not enter; here the people’s fault affects him [[nabre:deuteronomy/3]].

4.s: Moses urges Israel to keep God’s law and not make idols, for they saw no form at Sinai, only heard a voice. If they are scattered, God will receive them when they seek him.
4.d: At Sinai Israel heard a voice but saw no form [[bible:Deuteronomy 4:12]]. No image could show the invisible God, and an image might be worshipped in his place [[tosn:Deuteronomy 4:15]]. “A jealous God” means God is wholly committed and will not share his worship with idols [[nabre:deuteronomy/4]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 4:24]].

5.s: Moses repeats the Ten Commandments and recalls how the people asked him to hear God for them.
5.d: In Exodus the Sabbath recalls God resting after creation; in Deuteronomy it also celebrates Israel’s release from slavery in Egypt [[tosn:Deuteronomy 5:15]] [[bible:Exodus 20:11]] [[bible:Deuteronomy 5:15]].

6.s: The Shema: “Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God; Yahweh is one. You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.” Teach these words to your children.
6.d: The Shema (“Hear”) is the basic statement of Israel’s faith [[tosn:Deuteronomy 6:4-5]]. Jesus called it the greatest commandment [[tosn:Deuteronomy 6:4-5]] [[bible:Mark 12:29-30]], and quoted 6:13 and 6:16 when Satan tempted him [[tosn:Deuteronomy 6:13]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 6:16]].

7.s: Israel must not make treaties with the nations of Canaan. God chose Israel not because they were great, but because he loved them.
7.d: God chose Israel as his treasured possession by grace, not because they earned it [[tosn:Deuteronomy 7:6]] [[bible:Deuteronomy 7:7-8]]. The order to “devote” the nations to destruction (herem) is described in total terms, but it is historically doubtful that Israel ever carried it out literally [[nabre:deuteronomy/2]].

8.s: God humbled Israel in the wilderness “man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth.” Don’t forget him when you prosper.
8.d: Moses warns against pride: God alone gives prosperity [[tosn:Deuteronomy 8:1-20]]. Jesus answered Satan with 8:3, showing that people need God’s word more than bread [[tosn:Deuteronomy 8:3]] [[bible:Matthew 4:4]].

9.s: Israel will take the land not because of their righteousness; Moses recalls the golden calf and his prayers.
9.d: Israel takes the land “not for your righteousness” [[bible:Deuteronomy 9:5]]. Moses’s forty-day fast is like the fast of Jesus [[tosn:Deuteronomy 9:9]] [[bible:Matthew 4:2]].

10.s: New stone tablets, and “what does Yahweh your God require of you, but to fear Yahweh your God… to love him, and to serve Yahweh your God” Circumcise your hearts.
10.d: To circumcise the heart means an inner change, removing stubbornness and sin [[tosn:Deuteronomy 10:16]]; Jeremiah and Paul take up the image [[bible:Jeremiah 4:4]] [[bible:Romans 2:29]]. God “loves the foreigner”, and so must Israel [[bible:Deuteronomy 10:18-19]].

11.s: Love and obey God, teach your children, and choose between blessing and curse.
11.d: Egypt was watered by hand from the river, but the promised land “drinks water from the rain of the sky” [[bible:Deuteronomy 11:10-11]], so Israel would depend on God for rain [[bible:Deuteronomy 11:13-14]].

12.s: Worship must happen at the one place God chooses, and pagan shrines must be destroyed.
12.d: The place God will choose is the central sanctuary: first the tabernacle, later the temple in Jerusalem [[tosn:Deuteronomy 12:18]]. The book bears some relation to the “book of the law” found in the temple under King Josiah about 622 BC [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]], whose Passover followed “this book of the covenant” [[bible:2 Kings 23:21]].

13.s: Do not follow any prophet or relative who urges worship of other gods, even if their signs come true.
13.d: False prophets could imitate signs and wonders [[tosn:Deuteronomy 13:1]], so faithfulness to God, not a sign, is the test [[bible:Deuteronomy 13:3]]. Jesus gives the same warning [[bible:Mark 13:22]].

14.s: Clean and unclean foods, and the tithe, including the third-year tithe for Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows.
14.d: Every third year the tithe supported the Levites and others in need [[tosn:Deuteronomy 14:28]] [[bible:Deuteronomy 14:29]]. Giving a tenth was practised long before Moses [[tosn:Deuteronomy 14:22-27]].

15.s: Every seventh year debts are cancelled and Hebrew slaves released, with generous gifts. “there will be no poor with you” if Israel obeys.
15.d: Debts were cancelled every seventh year, protecting the poor from the powerful [[tosn:Deuteronomy 15:1-23]]. That the poor will always be with us is no excuse to ignore them, but a call to help [[tosn:Deuteronomy 15:11]] [[bible:Matthew 26:11]].

16.s: The three pilgrimage feasts of Passover, Weeks and Tabernacles; appoint fair judges.
16.d: Passover recalls the rescue from Egypt, Weeks the wheat harvest, and Tabernacles the years in the wilderness [[tosn:Deuteronomy 16:1-8]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 16:10]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 16:13-17]]. “You shall follow that which is altogether just” [[bible:Deuteronomy 16:20]].

17.s: Laws for courts and for a future king: he must not multiply horses, wives or gold, and must copy and read the law.
17.d: A king was not against God’s plan, but misuse of kingship was condemned [[tosn:Deuteronomy 17:15]]. Horses from Egypt and many wives showed reliance on human power [[tosn:Deuteronomy 17:16]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 17:17]]; Solomon later had both [[bible:1 Kings 10:28]] [[bible:1 Kings 11:3]]. The king’s “copy of this law” gives the book its Greek name [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]] [[bible:Deuteronomy 17:18]].

18.s: Priests and Levites; no sorcery or fortune-telling. God will raise up a prophet like Moses.
18.d: Moses had no equal among the prophets, so “a prophet like me” would be extraordinary [[tosn:Deuteronomy 18:15]]. Later Judaism awaited this prophet, and the New Testament identifies him as Jesus [[tosn:Deuteronomy 18:15]] [[bible:Acts 3:22-23]].

19.s: Cities of refuge, boundary stones, and the need for two or three witnesses.
19.d: One witness was not enough; two or three could confirm or challenge each other [[tosn:Deuteronomy 19:15]], a rule used in the New Testament [[bible:Matthew 18:16]] [[bible:2 Corinthians 13:1]].

20.s: Rules for war: exemptions for the newly married and the fearful, offers of peace, and protection for fruit trees.
20.d: Armies often cut down trees in war, but Israel must spare fruit trees, which would give food and shade in the future [[tosn:Deuteronomy 20:19]].

21.s: Unsolved murders, captive brides, the rights of the firstborn, and the body of an executed man.
21.d: Hanging a body on a tree was a shameful display after execution, not the method of execution [[tosn:Deuteronomy 21:22]]. Paul applies 21:23 to Jesus, who became a curse for us [[tosn:Deuteronomy 21:23]] [[bible:Galatians 3:13]].

22.s: Laws on returning lost property, protecting birds, building safety rails, and sexual conduct.
22.d: A neighbour’s straying animal must be returned, not ignored [[bible:Deuteronomy 22:1-4]]. Ploughing with an ox and a donkey together would not work, since they differ in size and strength [[tosn:Deuteronomy 22:10]].

23.s: Who may enter the assembly, hygiene in the camp, protecting escaped slaves, and keeping vows.
23.d: An escaped servant must not be handed back to his master [[bible:Deuteronomy 23:15-16]]. These laws taught Israel to treat others fairly, remembering their own rescue from slavery [[bible:Deuteronomy 24:18]] [[bsn:Deuteronomy 19:1-26:19]].

24.s: Divorce, loans, kidnapping, paying workers on time, and leaving gleanings for the poor.
24.d: The certificate of divorce was a concession, not a command [[tosn:Deuteronomy 24:1]]; Jesus discusses it [[bible:Matthew 19:7-8]]. Ruth gathers grain under the gleaning law [[bible:Deuteronomy 24:19]] [[bible:Ruth 2:2]].

25.s: Limits on punishment, care for the working ox, levirate marriage, and honest weights. Remember Amalek.
25.d: Paul applies “You shall not muzzle the ox” to paying those who serve [[tosn:Deuteronomy 25:4]] [[bible:1 Corinthians 9:9-14]]. In levirate marriage a brother married his brother’s widow to continue the family line, as in Ruth [[tosn:Deuteronomy 25:5]].

26.s: Firstfruits with a confession: “My father was a Syrian ready to perish…”, and the third-year tithe.
26.d: The “Syrian” (Aramean) father is Jacob: his mother Rebekah was an Aramean and he lived in Aram many years [[tosn:Deuteronomy 26:5]]. The confession tells Israel’s story from Jacob to the gift of the land [[bible:Deuteronomy 26:5-9]].

27.s: On entering the land, stones are to be set up on Mount Ebal with the law written on them, and curses read aloud.
27.d: Mount Ebal lies east of Shechem, with Mount Gerizim to its west [[tosn:Deuteronomy 27:4]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 27:12-26]]. The people answer each curse with “Amen”, “May it be so”, acting as witnesses against their own disobedience [[tosn:Deuteronomy 27:12-26]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 27:13]].

28.s: Blessings for obedience, and long, terrible curses for disobedience, ending in exile.
28.d: Lists of blessings and curses also close ancient Near Eastern treaties [[nabre:leviticus/26]]. The threatened exile came with the Assyrian conquest of Samaria in 722 BC and the Babylonian exile of Jerusalem in 586 BC [[tosn:Deuteronomy 28:36]].

29.s: The covenant renewed in Moab. “The secret things belong to Yahweh… but the things that are revealed belong to us.”
29.d: The covenant includes future generations, “those who are not here with us today” [[tosn:Deuteronomy 29:15]] [[bible:Deuteronomy 29:15]]. Grace is the foundation of the LORD’s relationship with Israel [[tosn:Deuteronomy 29:2-30:20]]. Paul quotes 29:4 [[bible:Romans 11:8]].

30.s: If Israel returns to God from exile, he will gather them and circumcise their hearts. “I have set before you life and death… therefore choose life.”
30.d: God himself will circumcise their hearts, a work of his grace [[tosn:Deuteronomy 30:6]]. Paul reads “the word is very near to you” as the message of faith [[tosn:Deuteronomy 30:12]] [[bible:Romans 10:6-8]].

31.s: Moses appoints Joshua, writes down the law to be read every seven years, and is told Israel will turn away.
31.d: “He will not fail you nor forsake you” expresses God’s faithful care [[tosn:Deuteronomy 31:6]], and Hebrews 13:5 quotes it [[bible:Hebrews 13:5]].

32.s: The Song of Moses: God is the Rock, faithful and just; Israel will forget him, yet he will have compassion.
32.d: “The Rock” pictures the LORD as strong, stable and reliable [[tosn:Deuteronomy 32:4]]. God’s plan was to save the nations through Israel [[tosn:Deuteronomy 32:21]], and Paul quotes “Rejoice, you nations, with his people” [[bible:Deuteronomy 32:43]] [[bible:Romans 15:10]].

33.s: Moses blesses the twelve tribes. “The eternal God is your dwelling place. Underneath are the everlasting arms.”
33.d: As Jacob blessed his twelve sons, Moses blesses the tribes that came from them [[tosn:Deuteronomy 33:1-29]] [[bible:Genesis 49:1-28]]. The “everlasting arms” speak of God’s eternal nature and care [[tosn:Deuteronomy 33:27]].

34.s: Moses sees the promised land from Mount Nebo, dies, and is buried by God in an unknown grave. No prophet like him has arisen since.
34.d: No one knows where Moses’s tomb is [[bible:Deuteronomy 34:6]]. An editor completed the book after Moses’s death [[bo:885]]. Moses shares in the glory of Jesus at the Transfiguration [[tosn:Deuteronomy 34:1-12]] [[bible:Luke 9:28-36]].
